orders.text:
SA 113/2015
Hon’ble Servesh Kumar Gupta, J.
Mr. Neeraj Garg, Advocate, for 
the appellant. 
Mr. S.K. Jain, Sr. Advocate, 
assisted by Mr. Siddhartha Jain, 
Advocate for the respondents. 
Heard. 
This second appeal is admitted 
for hearing on the following substantial 
questions of law: 
(a) Whether once plea of 
defendant no. 2 of acquiring title by 
efflux of time was declined and 
attained finality up till Hon’ble 
Supreme Court of India, plaintiff was 
entitled for decree even on the basis of 
title and defendant was liable to be 
evicted on the ground of denial of title 
of plaintiff? 
(b) Whether once plea of 
limitation raised by defendant in O.S. 
no. 346 of 1991 decided against him 
attained finality up till Hon’ble 
Supreme Court of India and operates 
resjudicata in view of section 11 
C.P.C., lower appellate court was 
justified in dismissing the suit of 
plaintiff/appellant on the ground of 
limitation? 
(c) Whether lower appellate 
court was justified in dismissing the 
suit of plaintiff with the finding that 
since rights of predecessor in interest 
of plaintiff already stood extinguished 
under section 27 of Limitation Act, 
plaintiff has no right to institute the 
suit, ignoring the fact that suit was 
instituted by plaintiff before regular 
civil court on account of involving 
question of title and was tried as  regular civil suit based on sale deed 
dated 14.5.1984? 
(d) Whether judgment and 
decree passed by lower appellate court 
can be sustained for want of framing 
and deciding points for determination 
as per Order 41 Rule 31 C.P.C.? 
Lower court record has already 
been received. 
List for final hearing in the 
m n f June o th o 2016. 
 
 (Servesh Kumar Gupta, J.) 
 28.4.2016 
 Prabodh

orders.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
 Hon’ble Justice Sri Rakesh Thapliyal
13th May 2025
Second Appeal No. 113 of 2015
Rajendra Prasad …............ Appellant
Vs.
New India Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals and anr. 
..….......Respondents
Counsel for the Appellant: Mr. Neeraj Garg, learned counsel
Counsel Respondents: Mr. S.K. Jain, learned Senior 
Advocate assisted by Mr. Siddharth 
Jain, learned counsel 
(Mr. Rakesh Thapliyal, J.)
1. The instant second appeal was preferred by the 
plaintiff/appellant against the judgment and decree 
dated 09.07.2015 passed by the IVth Addl. District 
Judge, Dehradun in Civil Appeal No. 20 of 2011, Smt. 
Aruna Dhamija vs. Rajendra Prasad and another 
whereby the appeal of the defendant/respondent was 
allowed by setting aside the judgment and decree dated 
09.02.2011 passed in O.S. No. 347 of 1987.
2. Certain relevant points have been placed by Mr. 
Jain, learned Senior Advocate on behalf of the 
respondents which certainly goes to the root of the 
matter. 
The defendants/respondents herein were earlier 
the tenants of one Shakuntala Devi and on 23.01.1968 a 
notice was given by her for terminating their tenancy, 
and, as such, on expiry of 30 days period of notice, the 
tenancy was terminated on 22.02.1968. After 
terminating the tenancy, a suit for ejectment was filed  2
by Smt. Shakuntala Devi in the year 1968 but the same 
was dismissed for want of prosecution on 26.06.1970.
Mr. Jain, learned Senior Advocate informed this 
Court that the order dismissing the suit of ejectment, 
filed by Smt. Shakuntala Devi was never been revived. 
He submits that after terminating the tenancy of the 
respondents/defendants by Smt. Shakuntala Devi w.e.f. 
22.09.1968, there were no relationship in between 
Shakuntala Devi and the respondents/defendants as 
landlord and tenant since at any point of time neither 
rent was demanded nor paid. He submits that not only 
this, though tenancy was terminated on 22.02.1968 and 
till 22.02.1980, i.e., for 12 years neither the rent was 
demanded nor paid even no fresh suit for ejectment was 
filed, and as such, Shakuntala Devi herself extinguished 
her rights over the property in question in view of 
Section 27 of the Limitation Act which reads as under:-
“27. Extinguishment of right to property.—At the determination of 
the period hereby limited to any person for instituting a suit for 
possession of any property, his right to such property shall be 
extinguished.”
3. Mr. Jain, learned Senior Advocate further submits 
that since, Smt. Shakuntala Devi extinguished her rights 
over the property in question in view of Section 27 of 
the Limitation Act, consequently, Shakuntala Devi 
extinguished her all rights to create any third party 
interest over the property in question. He submits that 
despite the fact that Shakuntala Devi extinguished her 
rights over the property in question, she created third 
party interest by executing a sale deed dated 
05.03.1980 in favour of Smt. Satya Dabar and 
subsequently, Smt. Satya Dabar also created third party  3
interest by virtue of sale deed dated 14.05.1984 in 
favour of Rajendra Prasad who is the appellant herein. 
He submits that creating third party interest by 
Shakuntala Devi by executing sale deed on 05.03.1980 
in favour of Smt. Satya Dabar after extinguishing her 
rights over the property in question itself vitiate the sale 
deed dated 05.03.1980 and since the sale deed dated 
05.03.1980 by virtue of Section 27 of the Limitation Act 
is null and void, and, as such, further execution of sale 
deed in favour of the present appellant by Smt. Satya 
Dabar by virtue of sate deed dated 14.05.1984 also 
become null and void.
4. In support of his submission first of all Mr. Jain, 
Senior Advocate placed reliance upon the judgment of 
Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of R.V. Bhupal 
Prasad vs. State of Andhra Pradesh and others, 
AIR 1996 SC 140 and particularly he placed reliance to 
paras 8, 9, 13 and 16 and submits that since the 
tenancy of the respondents/defendants was never been 
revived by Smt. Shakuntala Devi for a period of 12 
years, therefore, the status of the respondent/defendant 
is of tenant at sufferance and being a tenant at 
sufferance over the property in question he shall remain 
in possession until he is ejected by due course of law. 
Para 8, 9, 13 and 16 of the aforesaid judgment as relied 
upon by Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate are being extracted 
herein as below:-
“8. Tenant at sufferance is one who comes into possession of land by 
lawful title, but who holds it by wrong after the termination of the term 
or expiry of the lease by efflux of time. The tenant at sufferance is, 
therefore, one who wrongfully continues in possession after the 
extinction of a lawful title. There is little difference between him and a 
trespasser. In Mulla's Transfer of Property Act [7th End.] at page 633, 
the position of tenancy at sufferance has been stated thus: A tenancy  4
at sufferance is merely a fiction to avoid continuance in possession 
operating as a trespass. It has been described as the least and lowest 
interest which can subsist in reality. It, therefore, cannot be created by 
contract and arises only by implication of law when a person who has 
been in possession under a lawful title continues in possession after 
that title has been determined, without the consent of the person 
entitled. A Tenancy at sufferance does not create the relationship of 
landlord and tenant. At page 769, it is stated regarding the right of a 
tenant holding over thus: The act of holding over after the expiration of 
the term does not necessarily create a tenancy of any kind. If the 
lessee remaining in possession after the determination of the term, the 
common law rule is that he is a tenant on sufferance. The expression 
"holding over" is used in the sense of retaining possession. A distinction 
should be drawn between a tenant continuing in possession after the 
determination of the lease, without the consent of the landlord and a 
tenant doing so with the landlord's consent. The former is called a 
tenant by sufferance in the language of the English law and the latter 
class of tenants is called a tenant holding over or a tenant at will. The 
lessee holding over with the consent of the lessor is in a better position 
than a mere tenant at will. The tenancy on sufferance is converted into 
a tenancy at will by the assent of the landlord, but the relationship of 
the landlord and tenant is not established until the rent was paid and 
accepted. The assent of the landlord to the continuance of the tenancy 
after the determination of the tenancy would create a new tenancy. The 
possession of a tenant who has ceased to be a tenant is protected by 
law. Although he may not have a right to continue in possession after 
the termination of the tenancy, his possession is juridical.
9. The question then is what is the meaning of the expression `lawful 
possession'. This was considered by this Court in a leading decision on 
the right to grant licence under the Cinematographic Act and Madras 
Cinemas Rules in M.C. Chockalingam & Ors. v. V. Manickavasagam & 
Ors., [(1974) 2 SCR 143 at 152]. Rule 13 of the Madras Rules required 
the licensee in lawful possession, when he had applied for renewal after 
the expiry of the lease of the licensee. The Court observed thus:
"Turning to rule 13, even in the first part if the applicant 
for the licence is the owner of the property he has to produce 
before the licensing authority the necessary records not only 
relating to his ownership but also regarding his possession. It is 
implicit, that the owner having a title to the property, if he can 
satisfy the licensing authority with regard to his possession also, 
will indeed be in `lawful possession', although the word `lawful' 
is not used in the first part. It is in that context that the word 
`possession' is even not necessary to be qualified by `lawful' in 
the first part of rule 13. If, however, the applicant for the licence 
is not the owner, there is no question of his showing title to the 
property and the only requirement of the law is to produce to 
the satisfaction of the authority documentary evidence with 
regard to his lawful possession of the property. The word 
`lawful'. therefore, naturally assumes significance in the second 
part while it was not even necessary in the first part. The fact 
that after expiry of the lease the tenant will be able to continue 
in possession of the property by resisting a suit for eviction, 
does not establish a case in law slaw to answer the requirement 
of lawful possession of the property within the meaning of rule 
13. Lawful possession cannot be established without the 
concomitant existence of lawful relationship between the 
landlord and the tenant. This relationship cannot be established 
against the consent of the landlord unless, however, in view of a 
special law, his consent becomes irrelevant. Lawful possession is 
not litigious possession and must have some foundation in a 
legal right to possess the property which cannot be equated with 
a temporary right to enforce recovery of the property in case a  5
person is wrongfully or forcibly dispossessed from it. This Court 
in Lalu Yeshwant Singh's case (supra) had not to consider 
whether judicial possession in that case was also lawful 
possession. We are clearly of opinion that juridical possession is 
possession protected by law against wrongful dispossession but 
cannot per se always be equated with lawful possession."
This decision has been followed in many subsequent 
decisions of this Court. In Krishna Kishor Firm's case (supra), 
this Court has considered the controversy in a slightly different 
scenario. The facts therein were that the appellant-firm while 
running the Cinema Theatre on a licence granted pursuant to a 
lease by the landlords, one of the co- owners had agreed to sell 
his share of the property and another co-owner also entered 
separately into a lease. The question therein was whether the 
possession was lawful possession under the Rules. Giving 
various illustrations, this Court held that the lawful possession 
means legal possession which is also rightful or at least 
excusable. Thus that which is not stricto legalo may yet be 
lawful. It should not be forbidden by law. In fact "legal" is 
associated with provisions in the Act, rules etc. whereas "lawful" 
visualizes all that is not illegal, against law or even permissible. 
"Lawful" is wider in connotation than "legal". Although 
provisions in Specific Relief Act empowering a person or tenant 
to recover possession if he has been evicted forcibly by the 
landlord, may be juridical and not lawful or a tenant holding 
over is not in lawful possession unless landlord agrees or 
acquiesces in expressly or impliedly but that does not alter the 
legal position about possession of a person not legal yet not 
without interest. In considering the Chockalingam's case, this 
Court made a distinction between nature of the possession of 
the lessee after the expiry of period of lease and the nature of 
the possession of the lessee acquiesced in by the landlord. In 
that context, it was pointed out that the lessee before expiry of 
period of lease acquired lessor's entire interest resulting in 
drowning or sinking of inferior right into superior right. That is a 
right one of merger into another. It has been separately 
recognised by Section 111(d) of the TP Act. Similarly, a tenant 
after expiry of period of lease may be holding over and the 
lessor may acquiesce in his continuance, expressly or impliedly. 
That is from conduct into lawful. The other may be where lessor 
may not agree to renew the lease nor he may acquiesce in his 
continuance. Such a lessee cannot claim any right or interest. 
His possession is neither legal nor lawful. Such was the ratio 
of Chockalingam's case.
13. In view of the settled position of law, the possession of the 
appellant is as tenant at sufferance and is liable to ejectment in due 
course of law. But his possession is not legal nor lawful. In other words, 
his possession of the theatre is unlawful or litigious possession. The 
appellant may remain in possession until he is ejected in due course in 
execution of the decree in the suit filed by the respondent. His 
possession cannot be considered to be settled possession. He is akin to 
a trespasser, though initially he had lawful entry.
16. The High Court, therefore, was right in its conclusion that the 
possession of the appellant is unlawful. The learned Single Judge of the 
High Court [K. Ramaswamy, J., as he then was] in M. Kameswara 
Somayajulu vs. State of A.P. [1989 (1) APL] 82 (SN)] was not correct 
in his holding that at the time of renewal, the licensee need not 
establish his lawful possession due to omission in Rule 12(B) (1) which 
was followed by another Division Bench. The Full Bench has 
reconsidered the controversy. For different reasons given by us, we 
think that the conclusion reached by the Full Bench is correct. 6
5. In furtherance of his arguments Mr. Jain, Senior 
Advocate further placed reliance on the judgment of 
Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Eureka Builders and 
others vs. Gulabchand and others, (2018) 8 SCC 
67 by referring para 69 which is being extracted herein 
below:-
“69. A right in the property once extinguished by operation of law, it 
cannot be revived unless the law itself provides for its revival in a 
particular situation. Such is not the case here.”
By referring aforesaid judgment Mr. Jain, Senior 
Advocate submits that since Shakuntala Devi 
extinguished her rights over the property in question, 
therefore, no right is accrued in favour of the 
subsequent purchaser by virtue of two subsequent sale 
deeds dated 05.03.1980 and 14.05.1984 which was 
executed after the expiry of period of 12 years. Mr. Jain, 
Senior Advocate further submits that since as per the 
judgment of the Hon’ble Apex Court, the status of the 
respondent/defendant is of a “tenant at sufferance”
sinceSmt. Shakuntala Devi could not revive her right 
over the property in question, therefore, no rights are 
accrued either in favour of Smt. Satya Dabar or the 
present appellant for instituting a suit for ejectment 
against the respondents/defendants.
6. Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate also pointed out that 
earlier a suit was filed by respondent no. 2 Mr. D.S. 
Dhamijaon the basis of the adverse possession against 
the present appellant as well as New India Chemicals 
and Pharmaceuticals bearing O.S. No. 346 of 1991 
andthe same was decreed against which first appeal was  7
preferred by the appellant Rajendra Prasad which was 
allowed against which second appeal was also filed
which was dismissed and the matter went to the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court by way of Special Leave to Appeal
(Civil) No. 17436 of 2007 and even the leave was not 
granted and the same was dismissed on 06.04.2009 
with the following observations:-
“Before concluding we may mentioned that 
the answering respondent herein has also 
instituted Suit No. 347 of 1987 for eviction. That 
suit is pending even today before the Trial Court. 
Before us it was urged on behalf of the petitioner 
herein that apart from Declaration of Ownership, 
petitioner herein had also asked for permanent 
injunction from being evicted in the present Suit 
No. 346 of 1991 which relief was separate and 
independent from the other relief of Declaration of 
Ownership. We find no merit in this contention. On 
examination of the plaint we find that permanent 
injunction was sought only on the ground of 
acquisition of ownership by adverse possession and 
relinquishment of right to property by efflux of 
time and therefore both the reliefs were based on 
the same cause of action.
It was urged that the High court has failed to 
consider the scope and applicability of Section 27 
of the Limitation Act. We repeat that the plaint 
does not satisfy the ingredients of Section 27 in 
Suit No. 346 of 1991. However, it appears that 
answering respondent herein has instituted Suit 
No. 347 of 1987 for possession saying that the 
present petitioners herein are trespassers and in 
illegal possession of the Suit property. It is 
contention of the petitioner herein that even a 
tenant-at-sufferance cannot be dispossessed by 
the landlord/owner after expiry of 12 years in view 
of the provisions of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act. We express no opinion on this point. If so 
advised, the petitioner herein, who is the 
defendant in Suit No. 347 of 1987, may take up 
this contention in accordant with law, in that Suit 
(which is pending).
Subject to above, this Special Leave Petition 
stands dismissed.” 8
7. Mr. Jain, submits that the Hon’ble Apex Court after 
taking into consideration that the respondent who is 
appellant herein instituted suit NO. 347 of 1987 for 
possession over the property in question and therefore 
the petitioner who is respondent herein may raise an 
issue that even tenant at sufferance cannot be 
dispossessed by the landlord/owner after expiry of 12 
years in terms of provision of Section 27 of the 
Limitation Act and a liberty was given by the Hon’ble 
Apex Court to raise issue of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act in the suit bearing O.S. No. 347 of 1987.
Subsequently, respondent herein took plea of 
Section 27 of the Limitation Act in the suit filed by the 
appellant bearing O.S. No. 347 of 1987 which was 
decreed, against which the respondents herein preferred 
first appeal and the same was allowed and being 
aggrieved with the same, instant second appeal has 
been preferred.
8. Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate submits that the instant 
second appeal was admitted on 28.04.2016 on four 
substantial questions of law.
9. In response to the arguments, as advance by the 
Mr. Jain, Mr. Neeraj Garg, learned counsel for the 
appellant submits that the arguments of Mr. Jain with 
regard to the right of Smt. Shakuntala Devi over the 
property in question by virtue of Section 27 of the 
Limitation Act that she extinguished her rights over the 
property in question is thoroughly misconceived because 
the tenancy was terminated w.e.f. 22.02.1968 which is 
the admitted position and thereafter the suit for  9
ejectment was filed by Shakuntala Devi in the year 
1968, within the period of limitation in terms of Article 
67 of the limitation Act, i.e, 12 years. He further submits 
that though the suit was dismissed for want of 
prosecution and the same was not revived but the suit 
for ejectment was filed within the period of limitation 
therefore there is no question of applicability of Section 
27 of the Limitation Act. He also pointed out that the 
respondents herein instituted earlier the suit against the 
present appellant on the ground of adverse possession 
which was instituted on 29.05.1991 bearing O.S. No. 
346 of 1991 wherein the following reliefs were sought”
(A) Declaration that the plaintiff is the owner of the 
property described in the schedule at the foot of 
this plaint by virtue of adverse possession having 
seen perfected by efflux of time.
(B) Perpetual Injunction be granted to the plaintiff 
against the defendants from dispossessing or in 
any way interfering in the possession of the 
plaintiff and the said property.
(C) Full costs of the suit be awarded to the 
plaintiff.
10. Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate fairly submits that the 
sale deed executed by Shakuntala Devi was in fact void
ab initio since by virtue of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act, Smt. Shakuntala Devi extinguished her right over 
the property in question, therefore, there is no question 
to challenge the sale deed executed in favour of Smt. 
Dabar then to the appellant. However, the right was 
accrued in favour of the respondents claiming adverse 
possession over the property in question in which 
Shakuntala Devi created third party interest, and, as  10
such, there was no option except to claim adverse 
possession against the appellant herein who by virtue of 
sale deed dated 14.05.1984 became owner of the 
property though by virtue of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act that sale deed was void ab initio.
11. Put up this matter on 15.05.2025 at 3:00 pm. 
12. On that day, Mr. Jain, will advance his argument 
on the following issue:-
“Whether instituting the suit on the basis of the 
adversc e possession over the property in question 
against the appellant herein does not amount his 
admission that the appellant herein is the owner of

orders.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
 Hon’ble Justice Sri Rakesh Thapliyal
13th May 2025
Second Appeal No. 113 of 2015
Rajendra Prasad …............ Appellant
Vs.
New India Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals and anr. 
..….......Respondents
Counsel for the Appellant: Mr. Neeraj Garg, learned counsel
Counsel Respondents: Mr. S.K. Jain, learned Senior 
Advocate assisted by Mr. Siddharth 
Jain, learned counsel 
(Mr. Rakesh Thapliyal, J.)
1. The instant second appeal was preferred by the 
plaintiff/appellant against the judgment and decree 
dated 09.07.2015 passed by the IVth Addl. District 
Judge, Dehradun in Civil Appeal No. 20 of 2011, Smt. 
Aruna Dhamija vs. Rajendra Prasad and another 
whereby the appeal of the defendant/respondent was 
allowed by setting aside the judgment and decree dated 
09.02.2011 passed in O.S. No. 347 of 1987.
2. Certain relevant points have been placed by Mr. 
Jain, learned Senior Advocate on behalf of the 
respondents which certainly goes to the root of the 
matter. 
The defendants/respondents herein were earlier 
the tenants of one Shakuntala Devi and on 23.01.1968 a 
notice was given by her for terminating their tenancy, 
and, as such, on expiry of 30 days period of notice, the 
tenancy was terminated on 22.02.1968. After 
terminating the tenancy, a suit for ejectment was filed  2
by Smt. Shakuntala Devi in the year 1968 but the same 
was dismissed for want of prosecution on 26.06.1970.
Mr. Jain, learned Senior Advocate informed this 
Court that the order dismissing the suit of ejectment, 
filed by Smt. Shakuntala Devi was never been revived. 
He submits that after terminating the tenancy of the 
respondents/defendants by Smt. Shakuntala Devi w.e.f. 
22.09.1968, there were no relationship in between 
Shakuntala Devi and the respondents/defendants as 
landlord and tenant since at any point of time neither 
rent was demanded nor paid. He submits that not only 
this, though tenancy was terminated on 22.02.1968 and 
till 22.02.1980, i.e., for 12 years neither the rent was 
demanded nor paid even no fresh suit for ejectment was 
filed, and as such, Shakuntala Devi herself extinguished 
her rights over the property in question in view of 
Section 27 of the Limitation Act which reads as under:-
“27. Extinguishment of right to property.—At the determination of 
the period hereby limited to any person for instituting a suit for 
possession of any property, his right to such property shall be 
extinguished.”
3. Mr. Jain, learned Senior Advocate further submits 
that since, Smt. Shakuntala Devi extinguished her rights 
over the property in question in view of Section 27 of 
the Limitation Act, consequently, Shakuntala Devi 
extinguished her all rights to create any third party 
interest over the property in question. He submits that 
despite the fact that Shakuntala Devi extinguished her 
rights over the property in question, she created third 
party interest by executing a sale deed dated 
05.03.1980 in favour of Smt. Satya Dabar and 
subsequently, Smt. Satya Dabar also created third party  3
interest by virtue of sale deed dated 14.05.1984 in 
favour of Rajendra Prasad who is the appellant herein. 
He submits that creating third party interest by 
Shakuntala Devi by executing sale deed on 05.03.1980 
in favour of Smt. Satya Dabar after extinguishing her 
rights over the property in question itself vitiate the sale 
deed dated 05.03.1980 and since the sale deed dated 
05.03.1980 by virtue of Section 27 of the Limitation Act 
is null and void, and, as such, further execution of sale 
deed in favour of the present appellant by Smt. Satya 
Dabar by virtue of sate deed dated 14.05.1984 also 
become null and void.
4. In support of his submission first of all Mr. Jain, 
Senior Advocate placed reliance upon the judgment of 
Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of R.V. Bhupal 
Prasad vs. State of Andhra Pradesh and others, 
AIR 1996 SC 140 and particularly he placed reliance to 
paras 8, 9, 13 and 16 and submits that since the 
tenancy of the respondents/defendants was never been 
revived by Smt. Shakuntala Devi for a period of 12 
years, therefore, the status of the respondent/defendant 
is of tenant at sufferance and being a tenant at 
sufferance over the property in question he shall remain 
in possession until he is ejected by due course of law. 
Para 8, 9, 13 and 16 of the aforesaid judgment as relied 
upon by Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate are being extracted 
herein as below:-
“8. Tenant at sufferance is one who comes into possession of land by 
lawful title, but who holds it by wrong after the termination of the term 
or expiry of the lease by efflux of time. The tenant at sufferance is, 
therefore, one who wrongfully continues in possession after the 
extinction of a lawful title. There is little difference between him and a 
trespasser. In Mulla's Transfer of Property Act [7th End.] at page 633, 
the position of tenancy at sufferance has been stated thus: A tenancy  4
at sufferance is merely a fiction to avoid continuance in possession 
operating as a trespass. It has been described as the least and lowest 
interest which can subsist in reality. It, therefore, cannot be created by 
contract and arises only by implication of law when a person who has 
been in possession under a lawful title continues in possession after 
that title has been determined, without the consent of the person 
entitled. A Tenancy at sufferance does not create the relationship of 
landlord and tenant. At page 769, it is stated regarding the right of a 
tenant holding over thus: The act of holding over after the expiration of 
the term does not necessarily create a tenancy of any kind. If the 
lessee remaining in possession after the determination of the term, the 
common law rule is that he is a tenant on sufferance. The expression 
"holding over" is used in the sense of retaining possession. A distinction 
should be drawn between a tenant continuing in possession after the 
determination of the lease, without the consent of the landlord and a 
tenant doing so with the landlord's consent. The former is called a 
tenant by sufferance in the language of the English law and the latter 
class of tenants is called a tenant holding over or a tenant at will. The 
lessee holding over with the consent of the lessor is in a better position 
than a mere tenant at will. The tenancy on sufferance is converted into 
a tenancy at will by the assent of the landlord, but the relationship of 
the landlord and tenant is not established until the rent was paid and 
accepted. The assent of the landlord to the continuance of the tenancy 
after the determination of the tenancy would create a new tenancy. The 
possession of a tenant who has ceased to be a tenant is protected by 
law. Although he may not have a right to continue in possession after 
the termination of the tenancy, his possession is juridical.
9. The question then is what is the meaning of the expression `lawful 
possession'. This was considered by this Court in a leading decision on 
the right to grant licence under the Cinematographic Act and Madras 
Cinemas Rules in M.C. Chockalingam & Ors. v. V. Manickavasagam & 
Ors., [(1974) 2 SCR 143 at 152]. Rule 13 of the Madras Rules required 
the licensee in lawful possession, when he had applied for renewal after 
the expiry of the lease of the licensee. The Court observed thus:
"Turning to rule 13, even in the first part if the applicant 
for the licence is the owner of the property he has to produce 
before the licensing authority the necessary records not only 
relating to his ownership but also regarding his possession. It is 
implicit, that the owner having a title to the property, if he can 
satisfy the licensing authority with regard to his possession also, 
will indeed be in `lawful possession', although the word `lawful' 
is not used in the first part. It is in that context that the word 
`possession' is even not necessary to be qualified by `lawful' in 
the first part of rule 13. If, however, the applicant for the licence 
is not the owner, there is no question of his showing title to the 
property and the only requirement of the law is to produce to 
the satisfaction of the authority documentary evidence with 
regard to his lawful possession of the property. The word 
`lawful'. therefore, naturally assumes significance in the second 
part while it was not even necessary in the first part. The fact 
that after expiry of the lease the tenant will be able to continue 
in possession of the property by resisting a suit for eviction, 
does not establish a case in law slaw to answer the requirement 
of lawful possession of the property within the meaning of rule 
13. Lawful possession cannot be established without the 
concomitant existence of lawful relationship between the 
landlord and the tenant. This relationship cannot be established 
against the consent of the landlord unless, however, in view of a 
special law, his consent becomes irrelevant. Lawful possession is 
not litigious possession and must have some foundation in a 
legal right to possess the property which cannot be equated with 
a temporary right to enforce recovery of the property in case a  5
person is wrongfully or forcibly dispossessed from it. This Court 
in Lalu Yeshwant Singh's case (supra) had not to consider 
whether judicial possession in that case was also lawful 
possession. We are clearly of opinion that juridical possession is 
possession protected by law against wrongful dispossession but 
cannot per se always be equated with lawful possession."
This decision has been followed in many subsequent 
decisions of this Court. In Krishna Kishor Firm's case (supra), 
this Court has considered the controversy in a slightly different 
scenario. The facts therein were that the appellant-firm while 
running the Cinema Theatre on a licence granted pursuant to a 
lease by the landlords, one of the co- owners had agreed to sell 
his share of the property and another co-owner also entered 
separately into a lease. The question therein was whether the 
possession was lawful possession under the Rules. Giving 
various illustrations, this Court held that the lawful possession 
means legal possession which is also rightful or at least 
excusable. Thus that which is not stricto legalo may yet be 
lawful. It should not be forbidden by law. In fact "legal" is 
associated with provisions in the Act, rules etc. whereas "lawful" 
visualizes all that is not illegal, against law or even permissible. 
"Lawful" is wider in connotation than "legal". Although 
provisions in Specific Relief Act empowering a person or tenant 
to recover possession if he has been evicted forcibly by the 
landlord, may be juridical and not lawful or a tenant holding 
over is not in lawful possession unless landlord agrees or 
acquiesces in expressly or impliedly but that does not alter the 
legal position about possession of a person not legal yet not 
without interest. In considering the Chockalingam's case, this 
Court made a distinction between nature of the possession of 
the lessee after the expiry of period of lease and the nature of 
the possession of the lessee acquiesced in by the landlord. In 
that context, it was pointed out that the lessee before expiry of 
period of lease acquired lessor's entire interest resulting in 
drowning or sinking of inferior right into superior right. That is a 
right one of merger into another. It has been separately 
recognised by Section 111(d) of the TP Act. Similarly, a tenant 
after expiry of period of lease may be holding over and the 
lessor may acquiesce in his continuance, expressly or impliedly. 
That is from conduct into lawful. The other may be where lessor 
may not agree to renew the lease nor he may acquiesce in his 
continuance. Such a lessee cannot claim any right or interest. 
His possession is neither legal nor lawful. Such was the ratio 
of Chockalingam's case.
13. In view of the settled position of law, the possession of the 
appellant is as tenant at sufferance and is liable to ejectment in due 
course of law. But his possession is not legal nor lawful. In other words, 
his possession of the theatre is unlawful or litigious possession. The 
appellant may remain in possession until he is ejected in due course in 
execution of the decree in the suit filed by the respondent. His 
possession cannot be considered to be settled possession. He is akin to 
a trespasser, though initially he had lawful entry.
16. The High Court, therefore, was right in its conclusion that the 
possession of the appellant is unlawful. The learned Single Judge of the 
High Court [K. Ramaswamy, J., as he then was] in M. Kameswara 
Somayajulu vs. State of A.P. [1989 (1) APL] 82 (SN)] was not correct 
in his holding that at the time of renewal, the licensee need not 
establish his lawful possession due to omission in Rule 12(B) (1) which 
was followed by another Division Bench. The Full Bench has 
reconsidered the controversy. For different reasons given by us, we 
think that the conclusion reached by the Full Bench is correct. 6
5. In furtherance of his arguments Mr. Jain, Senior 
Advocate further placed reliance on the judgment of 
Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Eureka Builders and 
others vs. Gulabchand and others, (2018) 8 SCC 
67 by referring para 69 which is being extracted herein 
below:-
“69. A right in the property once extinguished by operation of law, it 
cannot be revived unless the law itself provides for its revival in a 
particular situation. Such is not the case here.”
By referring aforesaid judgment Mr. Jain, Senior 
Advocate submits that since Shakuntala Devi 
extinguished her rights over the property in question, 
therefore, no right is accrued in favour of the 
subsequent purchaser by virtue of two subsequent sale 
deeds dated 05.03.1980 and 14.05.1984 which was 
executed after the expiry of period of 12 years. Mr. Jain, 
Senior Advocate further submits that since as per the 
judgment of the Hon’ble Apex Court, the status of the 
respondent/defendant is of a “tenant at sufferance”
sinceSmt. Shakuntala Devi could not revive her right 
over the property in question, therefore, no rights are 
accrued either in favour of Smt. Satya Dabar or the 
present appellant for instituting a suit for ejectment 
against the respondents/defendants.
6. Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate also pointed out that 
earlier a suit was filed by respondent no. 2 Mr. D.S. 
Dhamijaon the basis of the adverse possession against 
the present appellant as well as New India Chemicals 
and Pharmaceuticals bearing O.S. No. 346 of 1991 
andthe same was decreed against which first appeal was  7
preferred by the appellant Rajendra Prasad which was 
allowed against which second appeal was also filed
which was dismissed and the matter went to the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court by way of Special Leave to Appeal
(Civil) No. 17436 of 2007 and even the leave was not 
granted and the same was dismissed on 06.04.2009 
with the following observations:-
“Before concluding we may mentioned that 
the answering respondent herein has also 
instituted Suit No. 347 of 1987 for eviction. That 
suit is pending even today before the Trial Court. 
Before us it was urged on behalf of the petitioner 
herein that apart from Declaration of Ownership, 
petitioner herein had also asked for permanent 
injunction from being evicted in the present Suit 
No. 346 of 1991 which relief was separate and 
independent from the other relief of Declaration of 
Ownership. We find no merit in this contention. On 
examination of the plaint we find that permanent 
injunction was sought only on the ground of 
acquisition of ownership by adverse possession and 
relinquishment of right to property by efflux of 
time and therefore both the reliefs were based on 
the same cause of action.
It was urged that the High court has failed to 
consider the scope and applicability of Section 27 
of the Limitation Act. We repeat that the plaint 
does not satisfy the ingredients of Section 27 in 
Suit No. 346 of 1991. However, it appears that 
answering respondent herein has instituted Suit 
No. 347 of 1987 for possession saying that the 
present petitioners herein are trespassers and in 
illegal possession of the Suit property. It is 
contention of the petitioner herein that even a 
tenant-at-sufferance cannot be dispossessed by 
the landlord/owner after expiry of 12 years in view 
of the provisions of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act. We express no opinion on this point. If so 
advised, the petitioner herein, who is the 
defendant in Suit No. 347 of 1987, may take up 
this contention in accordant with law, in that Suit 
(which is pending).
Subject to above, this Special Leave Petition 
stands dismissed.” 8
7. Mr. Jain, submits that the Hon’ble Apex Court after 
taking into consideration that the respondent who is 
appellant herein instituted suit NO. 347 of 1987 for 
possession over the property in question and therefore 
the petitioner who is respondent herein may raise an 
issue that even tenant at sufferance cannot be 
dispossessed by the landlord/owner after expiry of 12 
years in terms of provision of Section 27 of the 
Limitation Act and a liberty was given by the Hon’ble 
Apex Court to raise issue of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act in the suit bearing O.S. No. 347 of 1987.
Subsequently, respondent herein took plea of 
Section 27 of the Limitation Act in the suit filed by the 
appellant bearing O.S. No. 347 of 1987 which was 
decreed, against which the respondents herein preferred 
first appeal and the same was allowed and being 
aggrieved with the same, instant second appeal has 
been preferred.
8. Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate submits that the instant 
second appeal was admitted on 28.04.2016 on four 
substantial questions of law.
9. In response to the arguments, as advance by the 
Mr. Jain, Mr. Neeraj Garg, learned counsel for the 
appellant submits that the arguments of Mr. Jain with 
regard to the right of Smt. Shakuntala Devi over the 
property in question by virtue of Section 27 of the 
Limitation Act that she extinguished her rights over the 
property in question is thoroughly misconceived because 
the tenancy was terminated w.e.f. 22.02.1968 which is 
the admitted position and thereafter the suit for  9
ejectment was filed by Shakuntala Devi in the year 
1968, within the period of limitation in terms of Article 
67 of the limitation Act, i.e, 12 years. He further submits 
that though the suit was dismissed for want of 
prosecution and the same was not revived but the suit 
for ejectment was filed within the period of limitation 
therefore there is no question of applicability of Section 
27 of the Limitation Act. He also pointed out that the 
respondents herein instituted earlier the suit against the 
present appellant on the ground of adverse possession 
which was instituted on 29.05.1991 bearing O.S. No. 
346 of 1991 wherein the following reliefs were sought”
(A) Declaration that the plaintiff is the owner of the 
property described in the schedule at the foot of 
this plaint by virtue of adverse possession having 
seen perfected by efflux of time.
(B) Perpetual Injunction be granted to the plaintiff 
against the defendants from dispossessing or in 
any way interfering in the possession of the 
plaintiff and the said property.
(C) Full costs of the suit be awarded to the 
plaintiff.
10. Mr. Jain, Senior Advocate fairly submits that the 
sale deed executed by Shakuntala Devi was in fact void
ab initio since by virtue of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act, Smt. Shakuntala Devi extinguished her right over 
the property in question, therefore, there is no question 
to challenge the sale deed executed in favour of Smt. 
Dabar then to the appellant. However, the right was 
accrued in favour of the respondents claiming adverse 
possession over the property in question in which 
Shakuntala Devi created third party interest, and, as  10
such, there was no option except to claim adverse 
possession against the appellant herein who by virtue of 
sale deed dated 14.05.1984 became owner of the 
property though by virtue of Section 27 of the Limitation 
Act that sale deed was void ab initio.
11. Put up this matter on 15.05.2025 at 3:00 pm. 
12. On that day, Mr. Jain, will advance his argument 
on the following issue:-
“Whether instituting the suit on the basis of the 
adversc e possession over the property in question 
against the appellant herein does not amount his 
admission that the appellant herein is the owner of 
the property in question.”?
 (Rakesh Thapliyal, J.) Parul
